articles.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
articles.summary: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.
articles.content:
The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

New Geological Clues Narrow the Search

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

articles.personality_title: Scientists narrow down origin of Stonehenge’s mysterious Altar Stone
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Stonehenge is a famous ancient monument in England, built thousands of years ago. At its center lies a large sandstone slab called the Altar Stone, weighing six tons. For over a hundred years, experts thought this stone came from Wales, but new research suggests otherwise.

**What happened** – A new international study used advanced scientific methods to examine the stone’s makeup. Researchers compared tiny pieces of the Altar Stone with rocks from different places in Britain. They found that the stone likely did not come from Wales, but probably from northeastern Scotland. Although they have not found the exact spot yet, the study helped rule out many areas and focused the search on the Orcadian Basin region.

**Impact** – This discovery changes what we know about how the builders of Stonehenge moved huge stones long ago. If the Altar Stone came from Scotland, it traveled much farther than previously thought—over 400 kilometers (about 250 miles). That means ancient people had remarkable skills in moving and shaping heavy stones. The study also shows how careful science can solve old mysteries by using detailed clues in the rocks.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue searching in northeastern Scotland using the new geological fingerprint from this study. They plan to examine more rock formations to find an exact match. Finding the stone’s original location will help explain how Stonehenge was built and provide insight into ancient technology and culture.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New scientific research has narrowed down the source of Stonehenge’s six-ton Altar Stone to northeastern Scotland, changing long-held ideas about its origin and ancient stone-moving skills.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques réduisent l'origine mystérieuse de la pierre d'autel de Stonehenge
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Stonehenge est un monument ancien célèbre en Angleterre, construit il y a des milliers d'années. Au centre se trouve une grande dalle de grès appelée la pierre d'autel, pesant six tonnes. Pendant plus d'un siècle, les experts pensaient que cette pierre venait du Pays de Galles, mais de nouvelles recherches suggèrent le contraire.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une nouvelle étude internationale a utilisé des méthodes scientifiques avancées pour examiner la composition de la pierre. Les chercheurs ont comparé de petits morceaux de la pierre d'autel avec des roches provenant de différents endroits en Grande-Bretagne. Ils ont découvert que la pierre ne venait probablement pas du Pays de Galles, mais plutôt du nord-est de l'Écosse. Bien qu'ils n'aient pas encore trouvé l'emplacement exact, l'étude a permis d'éliminer plusieurs zones et de concentrer la recherche sur la région du bassin Orcadien.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change ce que nous savons sur la façon dont les constructeurs de Stonehenge déplaçaient de grosses pierres il y a longtemps. Si la pierre d'autel venait d'Écosse, elle a parcouru une distance beaucoup plus grande que prévu — plus de 400 kilomètres. Cela signifie que les anciens avaient des compétences remarquables pour transporter et façonner des pierres lourdes. L'étude montre aussi comment la science peut résoudre de vieux mystères en utilisant des indices précis dans les roches.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques continueront à chercher dans le nord-est de l'Écosse en utilisant l'empreinte géologique créée dans cette étude. Ils prévoient d'examiner plus de formations rocheuses pour trouver une correspondance exacte. Trouver l'origine de la pierre aidera à mieux comprendre la construction de Stonehenge et apportera des informations sur la technologie et la culture anciennes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une nouvelle recherche scientifique a réduit la zone d'origine de la pierre d'autel de Stonehenge au nord-est de l'Écosse, modifiant les idées anciennes sur son origine et les compétences des anciens pour déplacer de grosses pierres.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos acotan el origen de la misteriosa piedra del altar de Stonehenge
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Stonehenge es un monumento antiguo famoso en Inglaterra, construido hace miles de años. En su centro hay una gran losa de arenisca llamada la piedra del altar, que pesa seis toneladas. Durante más de cien años, los expertos pensaron que esta piedra venía de Gales, pero nuevas investigaciones indican lo contrario.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo estudio internacional utilizó métodos científicos avanzados para examinar la composición de la piedra. Los investigadores compararon pequeños fragmentos de la piedra del altar con rocas de diferentes lugares de Gran Bretaña. Descubrieron que la piedra probablemente no proviene de Gales, sino del noreste de Escocia. Aunque aún no han encontrado el lugar exacto, el estudio permitió descartar muchas áreas y concentrar la búsqueda en la región de la Cuenca Orcádica.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia lo que sabemos sobre cómo los constructores de Stonehenge movían piedras grandes hace mucho tiempo. Si la piedra del altar vino de Escocia, viajó una distancia mucho mayor de lo que se pensaba — más de 400 kilómetros. Esto muestra que las personas antiguas tenían habilidades sorprendentes para transportar y trabajar piedras pesadas. El estudio también demuestra cómo la ciencia cuidadosa puede resolver viejos misterios usando pistas detalladas en las rocas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán buscando en el noreste de Escocia usando la huella geológica creada en este estudio. Planean examinar más formaciones rocosas para encontrar una coincidencia exacta. Encontrar el lugar original ayudará a entender mejor cómo se construyó Stonehenge y dará información sobre la tecnología y cultura antiguas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Una nueva investigación científica ha acotado el origen de la piedra del altar de Stonehenge al noreste de Escocia, cambiando ideas antiguas sobre su procedencia y las habilidades antiguas para mover piedras grandes.
